Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery 110 (2008) 279–281
Case report
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
in an 81-year-old patient
Markus Kraemer ∗, Peter Berlit
Department of Neurology, Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach Hospital, Alfried-Krupp-Strasse 21, D-45117 Essen, Germany
Received 13 June 2007; received in revised form 7 October 2007; accepted 8 October 2007
Abstract
We present the case of an 81-year-old female with severe rigidity, stiffness and superimposed muscle spasms that represents the oldest
reported patient with progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Two associated autoimmune disorders (diabetes mellitus
and Hashimoto’s thyoiditis) were recently diagnosed. A paraneoplastic origin was excluded. The spectrum of differential diagnoses including
classic Stiff-Person syndrome and paraneoplastic Stiff-Person syndrome is discussed.

Keywords: Stiff-Person syndrome; Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus; Paraneoplastic Stiff-Person syndrome
1. Introduction
Stiff-Person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurological disor-
der which is characterized by muscle rigidity and stiffness
with muscle spasms.
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and
myoclonus (PERM) is characterized by additional neurolog-
ical deﬁcits, such as ocular motor disturbances, pyramidal
tract signs, dysphagia, dysarthria and neuropsychiatric
dysfunctions [1,2].
In both, SPS and PERM, association with other autoim-
mune diseases is typical.
SPS as well as PERM are diagnosed based on continuous
muscle activity in the presence of GAD antibodies [3].
2. Case report
An 81-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of
painful rigidity and spasms of the torso and proximal limb
musculature. The patient reported that three weeks before,
she had started to suffer from unexplained falls. She noticed
rigidity and spasms in her right leg spreading to the axial
musculature and the other leg a few days later.

Neurological examination revealed contracted muscles.
Her spine and both legs were rigid. Arms and neck were unaf-
fected. Painful spasms of increased muscle stiffness that were
superimposed on the rigidity occurred as well spontaneously
as they were exacerbated by external stimuli.
The MRI of the brain and the whole spine showed no
abnormalities. The EMG examination revealed continuous
motor unit activity of agonists and antagonists simulta-
neously. Three months earlier she had been diagnosed
with hypothyroidism. Due to increased anti-TPO antibodies
(1700 kU/L) (normal < 100 kU/L) we diagnosed Hashimoto’s
disease. She suffered from diabetes mellitus. Lumbar tap
showed an elevated cell count (53/3) (normal < 8/3) in the
cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) with normal total protein and
without evidence for an infectious aetiology. Because of
suspected Stiff-Person syndrome we measured GAD anti-
bodies, which were 56 kU/L in serum and 25 kU/L in CSF
(normal < 0.7 kU/L in serum). Some days later, autonomic
dysfunction with tachycardia, hyperhidrosis and arterial
hypertension made transfer to an ICU necessary. There was
a simultaneous watery diarrhoea with the onset of the new
symptoms. The patient underwent extensive screening for
neoplasia which was negative. Anti-Amphiphysin, anti-Hu,
anti-Ma 1 and 2, anti-Ri and anti-Yo-autoantibodies screen-

ings were all negative.
While therapeutic effects of intravenous immunoglobu-
lines (30 g for 4 days) were minimal, the treatment with

high dose corticosteroids (500 mg i.v. for 5 days) resulted in
some clinical beneﬁt with the relief of the spasms. A main-
tenance treatment with methylprednisolon tapering slowly
from 100 mg to 40 mg per day in combination with high
doses of benzodiazepines, baclofen and vigabatrin was help-
ful, although cognitive side effects were dose limiting. A
control lumbar puncture after 3 weeks showed a noticeable
decrease in the cell count to 9/3.
The patient was still unable to stand without support. She
was urine and stool incontinent and had developed moder-
ate dysphagia. Furthermore, she developed impairment of
conjugate gaze to the left in combination with vertical nystag-
mus. Sensory testing revealed hypesthesia of both feet. Two
months later an intrathecal baclofen pump was implanted.
A year later, the daily dose of oral prednisone had been
decreased to 5 mg, but she still required 210 /H9262g intrathecal
baclofen per day due to the residual stiffness. The muscle
tone and strength were quite normal in both arms. Additional
signs like hypesthesia and ocular motor disturbances were
resolved. The tone of lower extremities was still increased,
especially on the right leg. Yet again all examinations yielded
no hint at a paraneoplastic process. GAD antibodies were now
55 kU/L in serum and 27 kU/L in CSF, anti-TPO antibodies
were also elevated with 300 kU/L.
It was decided to continue the treatment with the 5 mg
daily prednisone and increase the intrathecal baclofen dose
to 240 /H9262g per day. A few months later her gait had sud-
denly become more unsteady. The rigidity of the right leg
had worsened but the other clinical and diagnostic features
were unchanged. The repeated search for an occult neoplasia
was negative.
3. Discussion
Initially the patient was diagnosed as having classic Stiff-
Person syndrome (SPS) associated with newly discovered
diabetes mellitus and Hashimoto’s thyoiditis. Advanced age
with subacute and severe onset and relapsing remitting
course, as seen in our patient, is uncommon for classic SPS.
It resembles subacute cases rarely published as “subacute
myoclonic spinal neuronitis” [3,4]. It is considered that this
disease is a more rapidly progressive form of progressive
encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)[1].
Controversy exists as to whether PERM represents a “plus”
variant of SPS or a different entity altogether [2]. Although
the symptoms stiffness, rigidity and spasms, seen in PERM
are similar to those found in SPS, PERM is characterized
by additional neurological deﬁcits [2]. In many cases, addi-
tional signs are mild or transient [1]. PERM is a variant with
increased mortality in which sphincter loss, autonomic failure
and cerebrospinal ﬂuid pleocytosis are more frequent than in
SPS [5].
Usually the onset of SPS and PERM is during the 3rd
to 6th age decade [1,5]. So far oldest reported patient was
72 years old [3,4]. Advanced age, subacute onset, rapid
progression and poor treatment response to diazepam sug-
gest paraneoplastic SPS [6,7], necessitating an intensive
screening for neoplasia. However paraneoplastic SPS is
not associated with GAD antibodies [8]. A prominent fea-
ture of paraneoplastic forms may be the involvement of
the upper extremities [1], the most important difference is
the presence of amphiphysin antibodies [6,9]. The clinical
appearance, neurophysiological and laboratory character-

istics in this patient were consistent with PERM. It is
hypothesised that SPS and PERM are part of a spectrum of
autoimmune-encephalomyelopathies that may occur even in
elderly patients.
In general, the immune system undergoes functional
changes throughout the years with gradually decreases with
the years, which is named immunosenescence [10]. Some
studies in healthy octogenarians and up showed an increase
in two contrasting phenomena coexist in immunosenscence:
a decrease in the capacity of the immune response and on the
autoantibody production [10]. An increase of autoimmune
manifestations may be the consequence of this progressive
aging of the immune system production [10].
In both, SPS and PERM, an association with other autoim-
mune diseases is typical [1]. Diabetes mellitus is found in
30–60%, autoimmune thyroid disorders in 10% and perni-
cious anaemia in 5%[1]. In the presented case it is interesting
that hypothyroidism was diagnosed three months before ﬁrst
motor symptoms and that both, the Hashimoto’s thyreoditis
and the diabetes mellitus were of recent onset.
High prevalence of raised GAD antibodies is not only
reported in SPS and PERM, but also in diabetes mellitus
and autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome [8]. Meinck et al.
[8] concluded that autoimmunity against GAD is not sim-
ply a non-speciﬁc epiphenomenon of neuronal damage nor
a common feature of a neurological autoimmune process.
According to Meinck et al. [8] antibodies against GAD may
be a pathogenetic agent or a marker for an ongoing autoim-
mune process or both.
Optimal management of SPS and PERM is still an
unsolved problem. This case report is an addition to the
limited pool of existing literature on SPS and PERM. In gen-
eral, Stiff-Person plus syndromes have a very poor treatment
response and prognosis. The main purpose of this report is to
present the treatment effect.
Diazepam is widely used as the standard symptomatic
drug treatment [1,11]. But increasing doses are often nec-
essary and so cognitive side effects may be dose limiting
[11]. There is a strong support for the use of intravenous
immunoglobuline and the duration of effect can be sustained
for up a year[1,11–13]. Also initial treatment with high dose
intravenous methylprednisolon (500 mg i.v. for 5 days) fol-
lowed by a maintenance oral methyprednisolon should be
effective [1].
Treatment experiences in this case support the hypothesis
of Meinck et al. that initial treatment with high dose methyl-
prednisolon followed by maintenance oral methylpresnisolon
is superior to intravenous immunglobulines [1,12,13]. This

is the ﬁrst documented case with a positive response to the
described treatment.
In summary this case demonstrates how important it is to
think of this rare movement disorder. The reported patient was
ﬁrst treated in an orthopaedic clinic and was misdiagnosed as
hysterical. More should be done to clarify pathophysiology
and treatment options of SPS and PERM. Clinicians should
be alert to the fact that optimal management is still a source
of controversy. Because SPS and PERM are very seriously
diseases there is little reason to withhold different treatment
options like immunoglobulines and glucocorticoids.
